title: Seedless Blackberries and Cherries That Grow on Bushes Vie to Be the Future of Food
gist: North Carolina startup Pairwise is using Crispr to stack multiple traits into crops at once — seedless thornless blackberries, pitless peaches, cherry bushes, multi-gene disease-resistant corn — and has pivoted from consumer brands to licensing, with Bayer, Corteva, Mars and Sun World as partners. The commercial reality lags the story badly: one product on sale (a blackberry in Colombia), a 70 percent collapse in ag-tech/food-tech funding since 2021's $50B peak, and only ~$3B invested in gene-edited seed startups over a decade.

themes.theme: Trait stacking as the real Crispr unlock

insights.claim: The decisive advantage of Crispr over conventional breeding is not speed but stacking — editing the best-tasting blackberry variety to be seedless directly, rather than crossing a seedless line with a tasty line and hoping the offspring inherits both.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: The moat in ag-biotech shifts from germplasm libraries to editing platforms plus trait IP; incumbents with seed banks lose relative advantage.
insights.quote: Pairwise didn’t have to cross seedless blackberries with the best-tasting blackberries and hope the seedless offspring taste good; they just edited the best-tasting variety to make it seedless.
insights.locator: The experts say Crispr is already at least 95 percent faster

insights.claim: Crispr is at least 95 percent faster than conventional plant breeding, and AI models that pinpoint where and how to edit genes are accelerating it further — compounding two exponential curves in crop development.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Development cycle compression from a generation to a few years changes the NPV math on ag-biotech R&D; watch AI-guided edit-site prediction as a distinct tooling layer.
insights.quote: The experts say Crispr is already at least 95 percent faster than conventional plant breeding, and artificial intelligence models that help pinpoint where and how to edit genes are further accelerating the process.
insights.locator: The experts say Crispr is already at least 95 percent faster

insights.claim: Conventional breeding is trapped by pleiotropic trade-offs — fruit bred to spoil slower may lose flavor or yield, rice bred to need less water may need more fertilizer — because corn alone has 40,000 genes creating near-infinite combinatorial variables.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Explains why decades of conventional yield gains plateaued; single-trait precision is the mechanism by which Crispr escapes the trade-off frontier.
insights.quote: If you breed fruit that takes longer to spoil, it might lose flavor or yield; if you breed rice that needs less water, it might need more fertilizer.
insights.locator: But even after the introduction of GMO crops

insights.claim: Pairwise's cherry bush shows a single trait edit can restructure the entire physical economics of an orchard — more fruit per acre, easier machine spraying and harvesting — and the underlying trait is not cherry-specific, so it ports to other tree fruits.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Platform-style trait reuse across species is the scalability argument; a single validated edit becomes a licensable annuity across multiple crops.
insights.quote: It’s exciting how one change can fundamentally transform how a food is grown
insights.locator: Just as an electric vehicle doesn’t have to look like a conventional car

insights.claim: Pairwise and Bayer optimized the number of kernel rows on an ear of corn and now plan to stack that edit with 'minor-effect' traits — shorter stalks against wind damage, heat and drought tolerance, more efficient fertilizer use — to compound into major yield and resilience gains.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: The accumulation of small edits, not one hero gene, is where yield uplift comes from — a slow-compounding rather than binary product story.
insights.quote: That’s the big unlock, this truly unprecedented ability to imagine the kind of corn we want and create it with speed and scale
insights.locator: For instance, after isolating the trait that controls how many rows

themes.theme: Pairwise's pivot from brand to licensing

insights.claim: Pairwise launched the first US Crispr food product in 2023 — a less bitter mustard green — and discontinued it in early 2024, then abandoned consumer branding entirely in favor of licensing its technology to others.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A direct-to-consumer gene-edited food brand failed fast; the viable business model in this sector is upstream trait licensing, not CPG.
insights.quote: Pairwise launched the first Crispr product in the US in 2023, a less bitter mustard green. It said it was discontinuing the product in early 2024 in favor of developing other gene-edited crops.
insights.locator: So far, the market for gene-edited food is almost entirely theoretical

insights.claim: Pairwise has more than 50 regulatory approvals for five edited crops across nine countries but only one product actually for sale — a high-yielding blackberry in limited quantities in Colombia — showing regulatory clearance is no longer the binding constraint on commercialization.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: The bottleneck has moved from regulators to breeding timelines, capital, and distribution — regulatory milestones are a weak signal of near-term revenue.
insights.quote: Today, the company has received more than 50 regulatory approvals for five edited crops in nine countries, but it has only one creation for sale, a high-yielding blackberry variety available in limited quantities in Colombia.
insights.locator: So far, the market for gene-edited food is almost entirely theoretical

insights.claim: Pairwise has raised more than $160 million and partners with Bayer, Corteva, Mars and Sun World plus universities — meaning the Big Ag incumbents are buying access to editing capability rather than building it in-house.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Incumbent partnership structure is the likeliest exit path for gene-editing startups; watch for outright acquisition of trait platforms by Bayer/Corteva.
insights.quote: It has raised more than $160 million, and ever since its short-lived experiment with non-bitter greens, it has focused on licensing its technology rather than building its own brands.
insights.locator: But the scientists who founded Pairwise believe

insights.claim: Pairwise's triple-trait blackberries will not reach US groceries before 2030, a five-year-plus gap between demonstrated science and consumer availability even with turbo-charged breeding.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Any investment thesis here must underwrite a half-decade of pre-revenue burn; near-term catalysts are licensing deals, not product launches.
insights.quote: Pairwise’s triple-threat berries won’t be in US groceries before 2030—even turbo-charged breeding takes time
insights.locator: That’s the promise of modern genomics

insights.claim: Pairwise CEO Tom Adams, who ran Monsanto's biotechnology work before the Bayer merger, deliberately targeted consumer-facing fruits and vegetables because GMO benefits like Roundup Ready row crops accrued almost entirely to farmers of animal feed and obscure ingredients, leaving consumers with no reason to defend the technology.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A deliberate lesson-learned strategy on public acceptance — consumer-visible benefit is the political insurance policy for the whole category.
insights.quote: We talked about how cool the science was, not what’s in it for you
insights.locator: In other words, it has benefits for consumers

themes.theme: Regulatory divergence: crops accepted, livestock blocked

insights.claim: Governments have largely accepted Big Ag's framing that gene editing is a sped-up version of conventional breeding, and even the EU — which restricted most GMOs — moved last month to treat most gene-edited crops as regular ones.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: EU liberalization removes the single largest historical regulatory overhang on ag-biotech and opens a market that GMOs never penetrated.
insights.quote: Even the EU, which has restricted most GMO’s, moved last month to treat most gene-edited crops like regular ones.
insights.locator: So far, governments around the world have largely accepted

insights.claim: The US FDA regulates gene-edited animals as if they were drugs and has required scientists to incinerate them after study, creating a regulatory chasm between edited crops and edited livestock.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Edited-livestock ventures face a fundamentally worse regulatory cost structure than edited-crop ventures; do not underwrite them on the same multiple.
insights.quote: the US Food and Drug Administration regulates edited animals as if they were drugs, and has required scientists to incinerate them after studying them
insights.locator: But regulators have been more cautious of Crispr livestock

insights.claim: Regulatory friction is already driving scientist emigration: UC Davis geneticist Alison Van Eenennaam, who created the first cattle embryos edited for more efficient male calves, is moving to Australia's University of Queensland where she can edit without restriction.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Talent and IP in animal gene editing are relocating to permissive jurisdictions — Australia becomes a watchpoint for the livestock-editing value chain.
insights.quote: People would rather have famines than technology that scares them. And if there’s no path to market, nobody’s going to invest in the technology.
insights.locator: The basic argument for caution is that we don’t know

insights.claim: Crispr's regulatory reprieve is fragile because the technology dates only to 2012 and could still be swept into the anti-Frankenfood backlash, with the Make America Healthy Again movement cited as a symptom of rising consumer discomfort with edible technology.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Political risk is the dominant unpriced tail risk in this sector; a single US consumer backlash event could reset valuations across the space.
insights.quote: Crispr was only invented in 2012, and there’s still danger that it could get swept up in the political and cultural backlash against “Frankenfoods” that has limited the impact of GMOs.
insights.locator: Unlike genetically modified organisms

insights.claim: Even industry analysts who consider Crispr safer and more useful than GMOs refuse to predict its commercial success, given that decades of scientific evidence never rehabilitated GMOs with the public.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Scientific merit has historically been a poor predictor of ag-biotech adoption — the analyst reticence itself is the signal.
insights.quote: even industry analysts who consider Crispr safer and more useful are reluctant to predict the success of the next revolution
insights.locator: Given the lingering unpopularity of GMOs

themes.theme: Incumbent commitment: Bayer and Corteva pipelines

insights.claim: Bayer deploys roughly 450 new crop varieties every year and its crop science R&D head expects every new variety within a decade to incorporate at least some edited genes — implying near-total penetration of gene editing into commercial seed by the mid-2030s.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: If credible, gene editing becomes table stakes in seed rather than a differentiator — value accrues to whoever owns the editing platform and trait IP.
insights.quote: Bayer says it deploys roughly 450 new crop varieties every year, and Graham says that within a decade, he expects every new variety to incorporate at least some edited genes.
insights.locator: Bayer says it deploys roughly 450 new crop varieties

insights.claim: Corteva spends nearly $1.5 billion on R&D annually and has made Crispr-based crop disease prevention its top R&D priority, targeting a 2030 corn product with four genes edited to resist four of the worst North American yield-eating diseases.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A dated, specific incumbent milestone: the 2030 quad-edit corn is a concrete checkpoint for whether stacked editing delivers commercially.
insights.quote: This is the holy grail, the ability to make the precise changes you want rather than searching for a needle in the haystack
insights.locator: Corteva spends nearly $1.5 billion on research

themes.theme: Capital drought and the ag-tech hangover

insights.claim: Investment in ag-tech and food-tech has fallen 70 percent from a 2021 peak above $50 billion, squeezing Crispr crop startups exactly when they need funding to reach market.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A funding-cycle trough with a real technology inflection is the classic contrarian entry point — but only for investors who can hold through 2030.
insights.quote: investments in ag-tech and food-tech have dropped 70 percent since peaking above $50 billion in 2021
insights.locator: The British startup Tropic Biosciences

insights.claim: The ag-tech funding collapse has two distinct causes — AI absorbing venture capital oxygen, and VCs feeling burned by former unicorns Beyond Meat and AppHarvest — meaning part of the drought is sentiment contagion from unrelated business models rather than a verdict on gene editing.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Mispricing opportunity: gene-edited seeds are being tarred by the failures of plant-based meat and indoor farming, which share almost no economics with them.
insights.quote: The dip is partly due to AI sucking up all the venture capital oxygen, but it’s partly because venture capitalists feel burned by the struggles of former unicorns like plant-based burger startup Beyond Meat and indoor farming pioneer AppHarvest.
insights.locator: The British startup Tropic Biosciences

insights.claim: Only about $3 billion has gone into gene-edited seed startups over the entire last decade, according to EcoTech Capital's Adam Bergman, who nonetheless rates them the highest-potential disruptor of the agricultural sector.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A tiny cumulative capital base relative to claimed TAM — either the thesis is wrong or the sector is dramatically under-funded relative to its option value.
insights.quote: there’s only been about $3 billion in investment in gene-edited seed startups over the last decade
insights.locator: EcoTech Capital managing director Adam Bergman

insights.claim: Food and farming are structurally hostile to venture capital because they are low-margin and slow, and Crispr crops must be created, field-tested by farmers, and distributed at profitable prices before returns appear — a mismatch with VCs craving quick high-multiple exits.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: The right capital for this sector is patient/strategic (Big Ag balance sheets, sovereign, philanthropic), not venture — expect corporate rather than VC funding to dominate.
insights.quote: That’s the thing about agriculture: Change is always slow, even with great tech
insights.locator: He thinks there’s some nervousness that the GMO story could repeat itself

insights.claim: Prior technological fixes for agriculture's land-and-emissions problem — vertical farms, AI-driven tractors, and plant- or cell-based meat substitutes — have all struggled in the marketplace, setting a low base rate for the gene-editing bet to beat.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Base rates for agricultural technology commercialization are poor; require evidence of unit economics, not just trait demonstrations.
insights.quote: technological fixes like vertical farms, artificial-intelligence-driven tractors, and less resource-intensive meat substitutes forged from plants or animal cells have struggled in the marketplace
insights.locator: Over the next few decades, the world’s farmers

themes.theme: Land, development and the democratization argument

insights.claim: The world is on track to deforest another dozen California's worth of land for agriculture by 2050 unless yields rise, which is the quantified environmental case underpinning the entire gene-editing pitch.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Frames yield technology as a carbon and land-use play, which opens climate-mandated capital pools to ag-biotech.
insights.quote: The world is on track to deforest another dozen California’s worth of land for agriculture by 2050
insights.locator: Over the next few decades, the world’s farmers

insights.claim: Gene editing is cheaper and faster than GMO development, which Tom Adams argues will make it a more accessible and democratic technology rather than one controlled by giant agribusinesses focused on commodity crops.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: If cost of editing keeps falling, the sector fragments toward specialty crops and smaller players — a different competitive map than the GMO oligopoly.
insights.quote: GMOs are extremely expensive to develop, which is why giant agribusinesses focusing on big commodity crops largely control them.
insights.locator: But gene editing is much cheaper and less time-consuming

insights.claim: Pairwise is working with the Gates Foundation and the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture on pest-, disease- and drought-resilient cowpea and cassava, and semi-dwarf Crispr yams designed to reduce labor for the African women who grow them.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Philanthropic co-funding de-risks smallholder-crop editing and builds political goodwill that offsets backlash risk in developed markets.
insights.quote: Gene editing can be such a powerful tool to help smallholder farmers
insights.locator: Pairwise is working with nonprofits like the Gates Foundation

insights.claim: The Trump administration's evisceration of USAID has ravaged the budgets of groups like IITA, directly threatening the pipeline that would deliver Crispr seeds to subsistence farmers.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: US aid policy is now a transmission channel into global agricultural technology diffusion — a geopolitical variable in ag-biotech adoption curves.
insights.quote: But the Trump administration’s evisceration of the US Agency for International Development has ravaged the budgets of groups like IITA, which could make it harder to get Crispr seeds to subsistence farmers.
insights.locator: But the Trump administration’s evisceration

insights.claim: British startup Tropic Biosciences is bringing a non-browning banana to market, but most Crispr crops remain at least a few years away from commercial availability.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: A second named near-term commercial data point to track alongside Pairwise for whether consumer-visible edited produce actually sells.
insights.quote: The British startup Tropic Biosciences is bringing a non-browning banana to market, but most Crispr crops are at least a few years away.
insights.locator: The British startup Tropic Biosciences

insights.claim: Pairwise's broader pipeline extends beyond berries to pitless peaches, disease-resistant row crops, and fruit and nut trees that first harvest within one to two years instead of three to eight — compressing orchard payback periods dramatically.
insights.speaker: Mike Grunwald
insights.so_what: Cutting time-to-first-harvest by 2-6 years transforms the capital intensity and IRR of permanent-crop farmland — relevant to farmland investors, not just seed buyers.
insights.quote: fruit and nut trees that produce their first harvest within a year or two rather than three to eight
insights.locator: The company is also working on peaches without pits
